title: Nonparametric Contextual Online Bilateral Trade
claim: A geometric picture of valuation space shows which image regions a structural lemma permits and which it forbids, motivating the algorithm's guarantee.
layout: 1 panel, square axes, shaded rectangles with overlaid blobs, dashed diagonal line
description: A single square plot of the seller valuation s (x-axis) against the buyer valuation b (y-axis), both running from 0 to 1, with a solid diagonal line b=s. A purple-blue block in the upper left sits above the diagonal. A yellow band lies below it, and a blue strip on the right overlaps the purple block. The price points p_L, p_U and p-bar sit on the diagonal. A dashed diagonal line marks GFT = 6h. A green blob lies in the purple and yellow region and is allowed. A red blob straddles both the yellow and blue regions and the dashed line, so it is forbidden. The eye goes first to the two bright blobs, green and red, against the pastel rectangles. Labels are minimal.
caption: The $x$-axis (resp., $y$-axis) represents the seller's (resp., buyer's) valuations. The blue (resp., yellow) region denotes valuations for which $p_L$ (resp., $p_U$) is rejected. [ref] states that if there are valuations both in the yellow and blue one, then there cannot be any with $\GFT \ge 6h=6L2^{-\ell}$. Let the green and red regions be the image of $\area(N_{\ell,z})$ under $(f_s,f_b)$, then [ref] forbids the red region, but allows the green one.
abstract: We study the problem of contextual online bilateral trade. At each round, the learner faces a seller-buyer pair and must propose a trade price without observing their private valuations for the item being sold. The goal of the learner is to post prices to facilitate trades between the two parties. Before posting a price, the learner observes a $d$-dimensional context vector that influences the agent's valuations. Prior work in the contextual setting has focused on linear models. In this work, we tackle a general nonparametric setting in which the buyer's and seller's valuations behave according to arbitrary Lipschitz functions of the context. We design an algorithm that leverages contextual information through a hierarchical tree construction and guarantees regret $\widetilde{O}(T^{{(d-1)}/d})$. Remarkably, our algorithm operates under two stringent features of the setting: (1) one-bit feedback, where the learner only observes whether a trade occurred or not, and (2) strong budget balance, where the learner cannot subsidize or profit from the market participants. We further provide a matching lower bound in the full-feedback setting, demonstrating the tightness of our regret bound.
